title: "Rejecting a Version"
tagline: "Or what to do when a specific version must never appear"

#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when a specific version must never appear*
This scenario demonstrates how to keep one specific version of a dependency out of the build, wherever it comes from. Maven has no "reject" keyword; the Maven Enforcer Plugin's `bannedDependencies` rule is the working substitute. Here `lib-b:2.0.0` is the version we have decided is unacceptable, and `lib-a:2.0.0` drags it in.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Maven 3.9**; the behaviour shown applies to Maven 3.x.
maven-enforcer-plugin 3.5.0 requires **Maven 3.6.3+**.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-a:2.0.0]
    LibA --> LibB2["lib-b:2.0.0 (banned)"]
    Root -- enforcer: ban --> LibB2
```

```{.xml include="pom.xml" snippet="s14-deps"}
```

```{.xml include="pom.xml" snippet="s14-enforcer"}
```

#### ! Expect
The resolver sees that `2.0.0` is rejected and picks another version of `lib-b`.

#### ! Actual
Resolution picks `lib-b:2.0.0` exactly as before; the ban does not take part in choosing versions. The build then fails at `validate`:

```
com.demo:lib-a:jar:2.0.0
   com.demo:lib-b:jar:2.0.0 <--- banned via the exclude/include list
```

#### ! Why
Maven has no resolution-time rejection. The Enforcer Plugin runs *after* the graph is resolved, inspects it, and fails the build if a banned coordinate is present. That makes the rule path-independent (it does not matter who pulled the version in) but also means it cannot steer resolution; it only reports. Gradle's `reject` takes part in version selection ([GS14](../../gradle-demo/scenario-14-reject/guide.qmd)).

#### ! Fix

```{.xml include="pom.xml" snippet="s14-fix"}
```

*   **Steer resolution to an acceptable version** with `<dependencyManagement>` (`mvn validate -Pfixed` here manages `lib-b` to `1.0.0`). The ban then never trips.
*   **Keep the ban** as the safety net that fails the build the day a new transitive brings `2.0.0` back.
*   **Ban a range, not a point**, when a whole series is bad: `com.demo:lib-b:[2.0.0,2.1.0)` is a version range in the `exclude`.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Banning a version with a published replacement and managing the graph to the replacement.
* MEDIUM Managing a library *down* past what a dependency asked for, as this demo does. `lib-a:2.0.0` was built against `lib-b:2.0.0`; test it against `1.0.0` before shipping.
* HIGH Banning without steering. The build fails on every machine with no path to green until someone finds the transitive and manages it.

#### ! Control
*   Always combine the ban with a version fix. The plugin detects; `<dependencyManagement>` prevents.
*   For organisation-wide policy, put the enforcer execution in a parent POM so every module inherits it.
*   Pair with `requireUpperBoundDeps` ([MS12](../scenario-12-metadata/guide.qmd)) so the fix itself cannot silently downgrade something else.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `mvn validate`, then `mvn validate -Pfixed`

**What to look for:** The first run fails naming `com.demo:lib-b:jar:2.0.0` and the path through `lib-a`; the second succeeds and `mvn dependency:tree -Pfixed` shows `lib-b:jar:1.0.0`.

**Conclusion:** The enforcer refuses the banned version; `<dependencyManagement>` is what actually removes it.

#### ! Scales
The Enforcer Plugin is widely used in enterprise environments for security and compliance. Organisations maintain parent POMs with banned-dependency lists updated as CVEs are published, usually fed by scanning tools (Dependabot, Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check) that identify the versions to ban.

#### ! Takeaway
Maven cannot reject a version during resolution. `bannedDependencies` turns the presence of a bad version into a build failure; `<dependencyManagement>` is the part that makes it go away.

#### ! Wild
After Log4Shell, the most copied enforcer rule in corporate parent POMs banned `org.apache.logging.log4j:log4j-core:[2.0,2.17.1)`: every 2.x release before the fixed ones, as a range. It did nothing to fix any build on its own. What it did was make every module that still resolved a vulnerable version fail loudly in CI, with the path printed, which turned a company-wide audit into a list of red builds that each owning team could fix with one managed version.
